# FDG9065

> DO implement the `IDisposable` interface by simply calling `Dispose(true)` followed by `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)`.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.4.1 Basic Dispose Pattern.

## How it is checked

- Check: sdk (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: CA1063, CA1816
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: draft

CA1063 reports a Dispose() that does anything but call Dispose(true) and then GC.SuppressFinalize(this), the reversed order and an expression-bodied Dispose() => Dispose(true) included, on externally visible types in the library profile and on all types in the application profile; CA1816 reports a Dispose() that does not call GC.SuppressFinalize on an externally visible unsealed type, and did not report an internal type even with api_surface all (probe with SDK 10.0.402). A sealed class whose Dispose() calls no Dispose(bool) is reported by neither (probe), so coverage is partial. Both also report the pattern that FDG9072 recommends: CA1063 asks to make the explicit IDisposable.Dispose that calls Close public, and CA1816 reports the Close method that calls GC.SuppressFinalize (probe); such reports are not violations. CA1816 also reports a DisposeAsync that does not call GC.SuppressFinalize, which is FDG9082's. Changing the body changes no signature, so autofix is no; neither diagnostic has a code fix.

## From the book

The call to `SuppressFinalize` should only occur if `Dispose(true)` executes successfully.

```csharp
public void Dispose() {
  Dispose(true);
  GC.SuppressFinalize(this);
}
```

> **Brad Abrams:** We had a fair amount of debate about the relative ordering of calls in the `Dispose()` method. We opted for the ordering where `SuppressFinalize` is called after `Dispose(bool)`. It ensures that `GC.SuppressFinalize()` only gets called if the `Dispose` operation completes successfully.

> **Jeffrey Richter:** I, too, wrestled back and forth with the order of these calls. Originally, I felt that `SuppressFinalize` should be called prior to `Dispose`. My thinking was this: If `Dispose` throws an exception then, it will throw the same exception when `Finalize` is called and there is no benefit to this, and the second exception should be prevented. However, I have since changed my mind, and I now agree with this guideline that `SuppressFinalize` should be called after `Finalize`. The reason is that `Dispose()` calls `Dispose(true)`, which might throw, but when `Finalize` is called later, `Dispose(false)` is called. This might be a different code path than before, and it would be good if this different code path executed. In addition, the different code path might not throw the exception.
